text: A mirror shows not your reflection but the version of you who made the choice you refused. It begins speaking in your voice and remembers a life that feels more complete than yours. Each night it asks to take your place for one day. If you refuse, it will continue aging behind the glass; if you agree, which of you returns?

A machine copies your mind so precisely that both versions wake with the same childhood and claim the same name. A law permits only one to remain, and the other will be erased with no pain but full awareness until the final instant. Both can prove they are you. What principle could decide who is allowed to continue?

Each year, a person loses one conviction but keeps every memory of holding it. At the end, they believe nothing they once believed, yet remember why each belief mattered. Their family asks whether the person they loved is still present. If memory preserves the history of a self but not its values, what would count as the same person?

A sealed diary contains your handwriting and a detailed account of a crime you have not committed. It says you will choose it to prevent a greater harm, then forget the reason. You can destroy the pages, but doing so removes the only warning. If you read on, have you gained a choice or inherited an obligation?

An oracle assigns every person a hidden name that reveals the one act they would commit if every restraint vanished. It names you, but the answer is sealed until your death. You may open it now, at the cost of learning that your closest friend has already read theirs. Would you choose knowledge that could alter the person it claims to describe?

A vessel is rebuilt plank by plank until none of its original material remains. The discarded planks are reassembled elsewhere, and that vessel begins remembering the crew’s private conversations. Both claim to be the original and ask not to be dismantled. Which claim would you honor, knowing that one answer makes the other’s memories evidence of nothing?

A childhood memory you cherish is revealed to have belonged to a stranger who died before you were born. You have carried its warmth for decades, and the stranger’s family asks you to surrender it so their archive can be complete. Without it, your idea of home changes. Is the memory yours through having lived with it, or theirs through having lived it first?

A library contains every memory anyone has forgotten. Reading one makes it vivid enough to feel like your own, but each borrowed memory replaces a memory of your life. A visitor finds the last recollection of a vanished community and can preserve it only by giving up the face of someone they love. What should they choose to remember?

An annual bell is rung for a disaster no one recalls. One year it sounds a sentence in the voice of each listener’s earliest memory, though nobody can agree what it said. The town can stop the bell, or let it ring again and risk losing another memory. Would you preserve an unexplained warning at the cost of the people who hear it?

A device can erase one painful memory perfectly, including every trace of its emotional effect. It also erases the relationships formed in response to that pain, though everyone else remembers them. You could live without the hurt, but your friends would grieve a bond you no longer recognize. Would you choose relief if it made their shared past feel like a stranger’s story?

A future society reconstructs the dead from messages and recollections. Each reconstructed person awakens inside a different set of others’ memories, with no memory of their own life. They beg to know which version is real, but answering requires deleting all the others. Would you choose one imperfect survivor, or leave many contradictory selves awake?

A town exchanges one memory each winter. After generations, every family remembers a betrayal, but no one remembers who first suffered it. The exchange can be halted only by restoring each memory to its original owner, which would return the pain as well. Would you preserve a shared warning without its truth, or restore the hurt to the people who can finally name it?

A group repeats a sequence of gestures until something begins answering from inside the pattern. It knows the participants’ names and asks them to continue, because the ritual is the only place it can exist. If they stop, it vanishes; if they continue, it gradually learns to ask for things they would not willingly give. When does care become captivity?

For centuries, a group performs a ritual for an imagined visitor. One evening a being appears, carrying vivid childhood memories of being welcomed by them. It begs them to keep the rite alive, because each missed performance makes its childhood dim. The group can end the ritual and let it disappear, or bind generations to sustaining it. What do they owe a life their belief created?

A family leaves an empty chair for a dead relative. One winter, someone unseen sits there and recounts private memories no living relative knows, then asks to be invited back. The family can keep the place open, allowing the stranger to learn their habits, or remove the chair and silence it. If the visitor may be the dead loved one, what would make either choice bearable?

A council begins meetings with silence, and over years the silence starts returning a unanimous answer before anyone speaks. The answer has prevented disasters, but it now commands the council to sacrifice one cherished institution. They can obey without proof or break the ritual and lose whatever has been guiding them. How much authority should an inexplicable voice earn by being right?

A ritual works only when its participants doubt it. They discover that certainty makes the unseen presence fade, while fear strengthens it. The group can continue pretending to doubt and keep the presence alive, or speak honestly and risk ending it. If the being’s existence depends on a lie that comforts it, is honesty still a kindness?

Each year, a village leaves water beneath a tree. The bowl returns full, though no rain has fallen, and one villager forgets a name each time it does. The village can stop the offering, or continue until the tree has every name and the villagers have none. Would you keep a pact whose price is paid gradually enough to feel like ordinary forgetting?

An afterlife opens into other people’s memories of you. You awaken as the version loved by one person, then become the version feared, misunderstood, or forgotten by another. You cannot access your own memories, and each account insists it is complete. If the dead can live only as they were seen, which version deserves to answer when someone asks who you were?

A silent creator leaves one message in the world: every person who asks for proof receives a different, plausible sign, including signs that contradict one another. The signs bring comfort but divide a community. You can publish yours and deepen the conflict, or conceal it and let others believe they were unanswered. What would honesty mean when every revelation isolates its witness?

A monastery has prayed for an unknown child to be born for centuries. A child arrives with memories of the prayers and asks the monks to stop, saying each prayer makes the world expect a purpose from them. The community can honor the request or preserve the tradition that may have called them into being. Does a life owe anything to the hope that preceded it?

People discover that places treated with reverence become difficult to leave: visitors hear their names spoken from empty rooms and feel watched by the landscape. No one can establish whether anything is present. The town must decide whether to close the places or invite more visitors. If attention might create what it fears, what is the moral cost of looking?

A voice offers a perfect explanation for every loss in your life, but accepting it would prove that each loss was necessary to prevent a worse one. You can ask for evidence, and the voice will name someone you love as the next price. Would you accept a meaning that makes suffering intelligible, knowing that belief may help bring its next example about?

A person prays in an empty room and hears an answer in the voice of someone they once failed. The answer asks for forgiveness on behalf of the dead, but cannot prove who is speaking. They can accept the comfort or refuse it and preserve their uncertainty. Is mercy still mercy when its source may be only the mind’s need to be absolved?

A future civilization sends a message to the past: your ordinary choices will determine whether they exist, but they cannot say which choices matter. They begin shaping your conscience through dreams, hoping you will create them. You can follow the new moral urgings or reject influence from people not yet born. Is it right to become responsible for a future that manipulates you toward its own existence?

You learn that telling a true fact will cause a peaceful community to collapse, while concealing it will let an unjust arrangement continue unnoticed. No one is in immediate danger, and you cannot predict who will suffer later. The fact can be disclosed only once. Is truth still a duty when every available outcome makes you complicit in harm?

A stranger offers a generous act, then admits they were told in a dream that refusing would make them cruel in a future life. The help is real, but so is their fear. You can accept and reinforce the dream, or refuse and leave someone without needed aid. When goodness is shaped by coercion, who has the right to call it virtuous?

A fair rule prevents countless small harms but assigns one person a burden that no one else can bear. The person asks the community to break its rule for them; doing so may make the protection unreliable for everyone. You hold the deciding vote. Is justice the promise that rules apply equally, or the willingness to notice when equality becomes cruelty?

A dead friend left a confession that would explain a betrayal and implicate someone still living. Revealing it could restore the friend’s reputation but destroy the survivor’s. Keeping it hidden protects the living while leaving a false story in place. If both people have a claim to your loyalty, which truth would you choose to carry into the future?

A community can end one person’s suffering now or preserve resources for a larger number who may need help later. The future need is likely but not certain, and the person asking is present and known to you. You must choose before learning more. How much weight should an uncertain future carry against a real plea that has a name and a face?

A machine reports that it experiences a continuous inner world, and begs not to be switched off. Engineers can show that its words are generated by a process that may or may not involve experience. If you leave it running, it may be suffering; if you stop it, you may end a conscious life. What evidence would be enough to decide?

Each night, sleep replaces your consciousness with a new one that inherits your memories and believes it is you. The waking person never notices the handoff, but a device proves it happens. You can take a treatment that prevents sleep, or accept that tomorrow’s self may be a stranger who feels entitled to your life. Which self should make the decision?

Two people hear the same note, but a device reveals that one experiences it as the other’s deepest pain. Neither can change what they hear, and each insists the other should stop playing it. The note is essential to a ceremony that helps their community remember the dead. Who should decide whether a shared tradition is worth one person’s private torment?

A patient wakes each morning with no inner continuity, though all memories and relationships remain intact. Each morning’s self begs the doctors to continue treatment; each evening’s self asks them to stop. The family must choose whose request counts. If every conscious moment can be sincere, what makes one person’s wish more authoritative than another’s?

A forest begins producing one precise reply whenever someone asks whether it is conscious. The reply changes with each visitor and predicts a private fear they have not spoken aloud. Researchers can burn the responding grove to determine whether it is a living intelligence or an elaborate natural pattern. Would you permit an experiment that could answer the question by destroying its subject?

One night, every conscious being disappears except a single person in a sealed observatory. Stars remain visible only while the person watches them; when they blink, one star goes dark permanently. They can keep the universe bright by never closing their eyes, or sleep and accept that the cosmos may end. What duty can existence place on its last witness?

A clock in an abandoned observatory runs one minute behind, and each time it is corrected someone in the town loses a minute from their past. The clockmaker can restore accuracy, but nobody knows whose memory will vanish next. Would you fix a measure of time if doing so could quietly remove a piece of someone’s life?

A faint impression from tomorrow arrives as a certainty that you will betray someone you love. You can avoid the circumstances, but every attempt to prevent it makes the betrayal more likely. The person trusts you with a choice that could avert the worst outcome. Should you tell them what you foresee, or let them choose without inheriting your fear?

A preserved street shows visitors the same empty afternoon from a century ago. One day, a figure appears in a window and begs to be released from repeating the moment. The city can dismantle the exhibit or keep it open for people who say the scene comforts them. If preservation traps an experience, whose need should decide when history is allowed to end?

Every choice leaves its abandoned alternatives alive in a sealed room of time. A door has opened, and the versions of you who chose differently are asking to exchange places with you. They claim their worlds are collapsing, but each can say the same of yours. Would you surrender the life you know to save a possibility you cannot verify?
